title: Sage
subtitle: The kitchen herb for throat and menopause: gargles, infusions, and compresses
excerpt: Sage is the strongly aromatic culinary herb whose leaves have a long western herbal use for sore throats, hot flushes in menopause, and as a topical preparation for excessive sweating. The fresh or dried leaves are prepared as a gargle for throat infections, a cooled infusion for hot flushes, or a compress for sweating. Dried sage keeps 12 months in a sealed jar.

glossaryTerms.definition: A herb or preparation traditionally used to reduce excessive sweating, including night sweats and hot flushes associated with menopause.

content.text: Sage in the home medicine cupboard, fresh or dried leaves as a gargle for a sore throat, a cooled infusion taken for the hot flushes of menopause, or an

preparation for excessive sweating. A kitchen herb with a long and consistent use in western herbal practice for mouth and throat conditions and, notably, for menopausal symptoms, particularly night sweats and hot flushes. Dried sage keeps 12 months in a sealed jar. fresh sage from the garden is available across most of the year in temperate climates.

attrs.title: Precautions
attrs.body: Not medical advice. Consult a qualified herbalist or doctor before use. Full precautions are in the 'When not to use' section.

content.text: Salvia officinalis L., family Lamiaceae. A woody subshrub, 30 to 70 cm, with soft, grey-green, pebbled leaves and purple-blue flowers from late spring into summer. Native to the northern Mediterranean coast. grown as a standard kitchen herb across temperate Europe. The leaf is the part used, harvested before and during flowering when the volatile oil content is highest. Dried well at room temperature.

The leaf carries a volatile oil (thujone, camphor, cineole) along with rosmarinic acid, diterpene compounds, flavonoids, and tannins. The tannins and volatile oil give sage its astringent, germ-fighting action. This makes it an effective gargle for sore throats. The sweat-reducing action, one of the better-evidenced traditional uses, comes from the diterpene fraction.

The herbalist Culpeper used sage as a gargle for sore mouths and throats. He also noted it for nerve tremors. The herbalist Grieve covered its use for throat infections and for heavy sweating. Current guidance supports sage for mild throat and mouth soreness (as a gargle) and for hot flushes.

Gargle: 1 to 2 teaspoons of dried sage leaf per 200 ml of just-boiled water, steeped covered for 10 minutes, strained, cooled to a comfortable temperature. Gargle for 30 seconds, then spit. Up to four times a day for sore throat. Do not swallow the gargle.

Infusion for menopausal symptoms: the same preparation as the gargle, but drunk as a cold or room-temperature infusion. One cup taken morning and evening. Start with one cup a day and observe the effect before increasing. Taken for several weeks.
Pregnancy and breastfeeding: do not use as a medicinal preparation. Sage has a uterine stimulant action and can reduce milk supply. Do not use at medicinal doses in pregnancy or while breastfeeding.
Epilepsy: thujone in sage stimulates the nervous system. Do not use medicinal sage if you have epilepsy.

Duration: current guidance and traditional practice support short courses for throat use (up to 7 to 10 days for acute infection). Longer courses for menopausal symptoms should be under herbalist guidance. Very long daily use of strong infusions is not the traditional pattern.
